When they expanded interleague play in 2013, they introduced some structure: you played all the teams in a specific division, which rotated from year to year. The exception occurs when the interleague division you play is the same one in which your rival plays. In that case, your rival simply becomes part of your normal interleague schedule. The two-and-two series, however, remains in the schedule (somewhat inexplicably) and is played against *another* team in that division.

The comics aren't canon. Just because a work is referenced doesn't make it an official part of continuity. As an example, a character's first name, which originally appeared in a promotional novel in the early 1980s, wasn't given on screen until much later. Does that make the promotional novel canon? It doesn't. It makes the novel's use of that name canonically correct.

I believe the creative team behind the reboot has made statements along the lines of "the tie-in comics are canon," but they don't have the authority to make that literally true. They are free to consider those comics as a part of the story they're telling, but nothing in them is part of official continuity unless and until it has been presented on screen.

It's not splitting hairs; that's how canon is defined. By the studios, by the networks, and by us. Canon is stuff on screen. There are some very good reasons to keep it that way: it's easier to maintain creative control when you're only worrying about one level of media, it's easier for producers and writers to adhere to it, and the other levels of media (such as print) aren't nearly as accessible to the public.

We - the studios and the fans - have all made a general agreement to respect that line (at least with regard to official canon...each of us is free to maintain their own "head canon"). When new producers or writers are brought in to make a new film or series, they are essentially given permission - by the studios and fans - to create new canon. When a fan rants about how much they dislike the new films, part of the reason is because they "must" accept those films as having equal standing to the rest of the canon franchise (again, individuals can decide what personal canon is for them...we're talking about official canon). The producers have not been given permission - by us or by the studios - to alter the definition of canon.

Again, the reboot team can draw from whatever sources they wish when making their films. I'm sure that in the writers' room there are giant whiteboards filled with background information about the world they're playing in, stacks of notes and charts and all sorts of things. If they want to publish some of that in comic form, no one is stopping them, certainly not the marketing department. I've read some of those comics and they're very good. I even incorporate stuff like "Countdown" into my own head canon. These comics are effectively their head canon. But they're not within the boundaries of what we've collectively decided is official. A producer can't change those boundaries just by saying so.

After the look of a certain alien race was changed, we were unofficially expected to just accept that they "always" looked like that. It's a misconception that what we see or hear in canon is necessarily what is actually being seen or heard by the characters.

One notable example is a trial scene in a well-known science fiction film. As the scene opens, we hear the aliens speaking their native language, and we are explicitly shown a clerk feeding the English translation into the main characters' headsets. Once the language barrier is established, the scene abruptly shifts and the aliens are now all speaking English. Did they randomly switch? No, because at one point a character says "don't wait for the translation." The film employs a conceit: it sets up that two different languages are being spoken, but then uses only the language we understand because translations and subtitles (and inventing a fictional language) is too cumbersome for the gravity of the scene.

The same conceit is employed in another episode where we hear a character speaking perfect English but the Americans hear a foreign language. This shows that the character doesn't speak English and never has; every time he has spoken in the series, he is speaking a foreign language that is being converted to English, not just by a universal translator but by the show itself. This must happen in any scene in which aliens are speaking to each other with no humans around: the bridge of a warship, a command room, characters bickering, and so on. The characters *can't* be speaking English, and so even though we hear English, we accept (as canon, no less) that they are speaking something else.

So if that's true for language, there's no reason it can't be true for visuals as well. This *must* be the case every time they recast a character, like a certain officer or a historical figure or pretty much everyone in a recent film series. Unless these characters all got drastic cosmetic surgery, it's taken for granted that we are to accept that the character "always" looked like that.

A normal analemma isn't especially complicated...you just take a picture of the sky at the same time and same place every day. I think most people use a tripod or something in their backyard that they just never move.

Including the totality of a solar eclipse takes a little bit more planning. Not just anyone can do an eclipse analemma, since eclipses only cover a small part of the earth's surface. Once you pick the spot, you have to know exactly when that spot will experience totality, and that time of day is when you start the sequence (you could of course start it on the eclipse day just to be sure).

As for the movements of the planets, that's the most fascinating part of astronomy to me, the clockwork of the cosmos, learning what *apparent* movement (what we see, like this analemma) has to do with *real* movement (what the system looks like from the outside). The usual example is seeing the outer planets slow down and reverse direction (over many months, measured by their position with respect to background stars)...this perplexed humanity until we finally figured out it was because they were in superior orbits and we were "passing" them (the inner planets do it too but for slightly different reasons and it's harder to notice).

You'll often see people talk highly of ancient cultures like those in the Nile Valley or Mesoamerica because they had "figured out" planetary movements, eclipse prediction, and so on. But they weren't any smarter, or had any more knowledge, than you or I. If you don't know anything about cosmic clockwork, it's because you spend your nights indoors watching TV. The cosmos was all they had. And once they figured out how to time agriculture to it, learning visual astronomy was critical to them. They knew Mars went retrograde and they knew when it would happen and for how long, but they didn't have any idea *why* it did. They didn't even know what Mars *was.* It was just a dot in the sky. They learned an extraordinary amount about the workings of the solar system with just their eyes and brains, but in the end it was all relatively obvious compared to what we've learned since the invention of the telescope and the development of modern sciences.

But the boxscore doesn't give a complete view of what the game was like back then. The pitcher was obligated to throw what the batter wanted; the artistry came in pitching to contact rather than trickery (there were no breaking balls to speak of). In 1871, three balls made a walk, but a ball was called at the discretion of the umpire if he determined that the pitcher was *repeatedly* not hitting the mark. There was no mound. All four bases were square and set entirely within the corners of the infield (today, second base is offset, centered on the corner...not many people realize that). The home team could decide to bat first, and often only one ball was provided for the whole game. Many of these rules persisted well into the era of the National League, showing that even with a relatively sound organizational structure, baseball was still in the process of figuring itself out.

One team lasted only a season, playing a total of 19 games, going 7-12. Their opponent managed a record of 16-35 over two years. The league was a loose, shifting amalgam of professional clubs (it is often not counted as a "major league"), but there were two franchises of note: one team, an offshoot of the original ballclub that dominated the standings, and another team, who legitimately challenged the first team although they had to sit out two years when their ballpark burned down in a major fire. These two franchises made it into the National League, and are still playing today as, respectively, a team in the Southeast and a team in the Midwest.
